title: Darjeeling Toy Train: Joyrides, Fares and Booking
meta_description: How to ride the Darjeeling toy train: steam vs diesel joyrides, the full NJP line, IRCTC booking, indicative fares, where to sit and monsoon disruptions.
summary: Most visitors ride the toy train as a two-hour joyride from Darjeeling to Ghoom and back, by steam (about ₹1,500–1,800) or diesel (about ₹1,000–1,300), booked on IRCTC. The full 88 km line from NJP takes most of a day and is often cut by monsoon landslides, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: A railway built up a mountain in 1881
paras: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, the toy train everyone talks about, reached Darjeeling in 1881. Before it, tea chests, rice and visitors came up the Hill Cart Road by bullock cart and pony, a slow and expensive climb from the plains. The railway's builders laid track only 610 mm wide, two feet between the rails, so that the line could follow the road and turn on curves a normal railway could never take.

The line runs 88 km from New Jalpaiguri (NJP), near Siliguri, to Darjeeling, climbing from the plains to more than 2,000 m. To gain that height it uses tight loops and zig-zag reverses, where the train runs forward up one leg, stops, then backs up the next. The Batasia Loop, the spiral just below Ghoom, was added in 1919 to ease the gradient on the last stretch. Ghum station, at 2,258 m, is the highest point on the whole line and one of the highest railway stations in India.

In 1999 UNESCO listed the railway as a World Heritage Site; the Nilgiri and Kalka–Shimla lines were later added to the same listing as the Mountain Railways of India. The little blue steam engines still work the joyrides, the oldest of them more than a century old, and the sheds at Darjeeling station let you watch the crews coal and water them in the morning.

sections.heading: Full line, steam joyride or diesel joyride
paras: There are three ways to ride, and they are very different trips. The full line from NJP to Darjeeling is a day out in its own right: seven to eight hours or more, through Sukna's forest, the loops above Rangtong and Tindharia, Kurseong's bazaar and Sonada, with the train crossing the road again and again. It is slow, crowded at stations, and the best way to understand why people love this railway. In recent years it has mostly run with diesel engines and has been suspended for long stretches after landslides, so check current status before you travel.

The joyrides are short return trips from Darjeeling to Ghoom and back, about two hours. They stop for roughly 10 minutes at the Batasia Loop for photographs and for about half an hour at Ghum station, long enough to see the small railway museum on the platform. The steam joyride is the one most people want: a coal-fired engine, smoke, whistle and the smell of hot oil. The diesel joyride follows the same route and timings for less money and is the easier ticket to get in peak season.

If you only have one day, we suggest the steam joyride in the morning when the light is clean and the mountains are more likely to be out. If you love railways, take the full line one way and a shared jeep the other.
list: Fares are indicative for 2025–26 and include reservation charges; the railway revises them, so check current status before you travel.
Joyride departures run several times a day in season and fewer in the monsoon and deep winter.

sections.heading: How to book on IRCTC
paras: All three services are sold through IRCTC, the Indian Railways booking website and app, like any other train. Search with Darjeeling (station code DJ) as both the origin and destination for joyrides, or NJP to DJ for the full line. Joyrides appear as separate numbered special trains for each departure time, and the steam and diesel runs are listed separately, so read the train name before you pay.

You need an IRCTC account to book, and a photo ID that matches the name on the ticket when you board. Foreign visitors can register on IRCTC too, though the process takes a little longer. Seats sell out weeks ahead in October, the Puja holidays, late December and May–June, so book as soon as your dates are firm. Outside those months you can often get a joyride seat a few days ahead.

If the website shows nothing, try the reservation counter at Darjeeling station the day before or early in the morning. Cancellations do free up seats. Avoid people on the street offering to get you tickets at a premium: there is no secret quota they can reach that you cannot.

sections.heading: Where to sit and what to watch for
paras: On the joyride the carriages are small, and every seat is close to a window. Because the line twists and crosses the Hill Cart Road, views change sides constantly, so neither side is clearly better. The big view of the trip comes at the Batasia Loop stop itself, where Kanchenjunga, at 8,586 m, stands behind the war memorial on clear mornings from October to early December and in March and April.

On the full line, sit facing forward if you can, and on the downhill run from Darjeeling be ready on the open stretches past Kurseong where the line drops toward Tindharia and the plains spread out below. Watch for the zig-zag reverses, where the train stops, a staff member changes the points and the train backs uphill. At Ghoom, and in Sonada and Kurseong, the train runs right through the bazaar, so close to shop fronts that vendors step back as it passes.

sections.heading: Photo spots along the line
paras: You do not need a ticket to photograph the train. Some of the best pictures are taken from the road, and the timetable tells you when to wait.
list: Batasia Loop: the classic shot of the train circling the memorial garden, with the mountains behind in clear weather; small entry fee of about ₹20–50.
Ghum station: the engine taking water, and the museum's old rolling stock on the platform.
Ghoom bazaar: the train squeezing between shops and parked jeeps on the main road.
Darjeeling station sheds: crews preparing steam engines in the early morning before the first joyride.
Kurseong station and the bazaar: the line runs through the middle of town.
Agony Point and the loops near Tindharia: worth a stop if you drive up the Hill Cart Road and the line is open.

sections.heading: Monsoon, landslides and disruptions
paras: The railway is built on steep, soft hillsides, and the monsoon from June to September brings most of Darjeeling's roughly 3,000 mm of rain a year. Landslides block the line regularly, especially on the lower section between Tindharia and Kurseong. Slips near Paglajhora have cut the full line for long periods in the past, and services between NJP and Darjeeling have been run in pieces, suspended or replaced at short notice.

The joyrides between Darjeeling and Ghoom are the most reliable part of the system and usually run through the year, with fewer departures in heavy rain. Even so, plan as if any train could be cancelled. Book a joyride early in your stay so you have a spare day to retry, keep your jeep or car plans flexible if you are counting on the full line, and check current status before you travel. IRCTC refunds tickets on cancelled trains, but money is not much comfort when your one free morning is gone.

sections.heading: Small things that make the ride better
list: Reach Darjeeling station 20–30 minutes early; joyrides leave on time and boarding is slow.
Carry a jacket even in May: the carriages are open to the wind at Ghoom, which is cooler than town.
Take the first steam departure of the day for clearer air and a better chance of seeing the mountains.
Keep some cash for the Ghoom museum, tea and the Batasia entry if your ticket does not cover it.
Children love the steam engine, but the smoke and soot are real; avoid white clothes.

faqs.q: Which is better, the steam or diesel toy train joyride?
faqs.a: The steam joyride is better if you want the full experience of smoke, whistle and the old engine at work, and it costs about ₹1,500–1,800 a seat. The diesel joyride follows the same Darjeeling–Ghoom–Darjeeling route with the same stops at Batasia and Ghum for about ₹1,000–1,300. If the steam ride is sold out, the diesel ride still gives you the loop, the museum and the views.

faqs.q: How long is the Darjeeling toy train joyride?
faqs.a: The joyride takes about two hours from Darjeeling station and back. That includes a stop of around 10 minutes at the Batasia Loop for photographs and about half an hour at Ghum station, where you can see the small railway museum. Timings vary slightly by departure and season, and services can be reduced in heavy rain, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I book toy train tickets for Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Book on the IRCTC website or app like any Indian Railways train. For joyrides, search Darjeeling (DJ) to Darjeeling; for the full line, search NJP to DJ. Joyrides appear as separate special trains for each departure, with steam and diesel listed separately. You need an IRCTC account and matching photo ID. If nothing shows online, try the Darjeeling station counter early in the morning.

faqs.q: How far in advance should I book the toy train?
faqs.a: For October, the Puja holidays, Christmas and New Year week, and the May–June school holidays, book as soon as your dates are firm, ideally several weeks ahead. Steam joyrides sell out first. In the quieter months of February, July, August and early September you can often find seats a few days ahead. Cancellations do release seats, so keep checking IRCTC if a date shows waitlisted.

faqs.q: Does the toy train run all the way from NJP to Darjeeling?
faqs.a: It does when the line is open, covering 88 km in seven to eight hours or more. But the full service has often been suspended or run in sections after landslides, especially between Tindharia and Kurseong, and it has mostly used diesel engines in recent years. Check current status before you travel, and keep a shared jeep (₹250–350 a seat) as your backup.

faqs.q: Is the toy train worth it for families with small children?
faqs.a: Yes, the joyride suits families well: it is only two hours, the stops at Batasia and Ghoom break it up, and children usually love the steam engine. The full NJP line is a long day for small children, with few toilets and slow stretches. Carry snacks, water and a warm layer, and keep children away from open doors and windows on the curves.

faqs.q: Does the toy train run in the monsoon?
faqs.a: The Darjeeling–Ghoom joyrides usually keep running in the monsoon, though with fewer departures and the occasional cancellation for heavy rain or track work. The full line from NJP is far more likely to be disrupted by landslides from June to September. If the train is central to your trip, plan a spare day, book early in your stay and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see Kanchenjunga from the toy train?
faqs.a: On a clear morning, yes. The best view comes during the stop at the Batasia Loop, where Kanchenjunga rises behind the memorial garden. Your chances are highest from October to early December and in March and April. From June to September cloud usually hides the range. An early departure gives you clearer air than the afternoon runs, when mist often rolls up from the valleys.

faqs.q: Why is the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faqs.a: UNESCO listed it in 1999 as an outstanding early example of a hill passenger railway, built with simple engineering to climb steep mountain terrain. Its 610 mm track, loops such as Batasia (1919) and zig-zag reverses carried it from the plains to Ghum at 2,258 m, and it is still working on its original alignment, with steam engines in daily use on the joyrides.
